description_full: Azbil Corporation provides automation products and services worldwide. It operates through three segments: Building Automation Business, Advanced Automation Business, Life Automation Business, and others. The Building Automation Business segment offers indoor temperature and humidity sensors, ceiling temperature sensors, indoor temperature and humidity controllers, infrared array sensors, workplace sensors, digital setting devices, marcellia-compatible user terminals, integrated user terminals, building automation systems, access control systems, contactless IC card readers, air conditioning equipment controllers, heat source equipment systems, air conditioning equipment, and control functions, etc.; and control valves, graphical controllers, digital mass flow controllers, instrumentation network modules, differential pressure transmitters, electromagnetic flow meters, and smart valves. The Advanced Automation Business segment offers positioners, collaborative automation systems, process controllers, adjustable proximity sensors, photoelectric switch, advanced UV sensor, limit switch, thermal micro liquid flow meter, dynamic monitoring system, online abnormality detection system, cloud services, ultrasonic gas meters, diaphragm smart meters, smart meter, and microcomputer meter. The Life Automation Business Segment offers pressure governor, battery-powered electromagnetic water meter, electronic water meter, air conditioning systems, whole-house air purification and ventilation systems, system, whole-building air purification and ventilation system, etc., and insurance agency software development services, etc. The company was formerly known as Yamatake Corporation and changed its name to Azbil Corporation in April 2012. Azbil Corporation was founded in 1906 and is headquartered in Tokyo, Japan.

financial_summary: AZBIL CORP is a mid-cap industrials business with a $4.8B market cap on $1.9B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at -1% over the past three years — essentially flat, and a business treading water is rarely a path to compounding.
Returns on capital run at 19% against a 9% cost of capital — a 10-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat, with gross margins sitting at 43%.

The business throws off $187M in free cash flow — roughly 10 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, with adequate 0.99× cash conversion.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year.
Shareholder yield of 4.3% reflects a genuine commitment to returning capital rather than empire-building, and insiders hold 4.5% of the shares.
